title: In-situ and Ex-situ Conservation: Protected Areas

cards.b:
Questions on national parks, biosphere reserves, tiger reserves and World Heritage Sites come almost every year. Mains asks about conflict between people and protected areas.

The key is to know which law creates which category.

A simple way to remember is by layers: legal categories under the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, then UNESCO designations such as biosphere reserves and World Heritage Sites, then ex-situ centres. Conflict questions often involve relocation of villages, forest rights under the 2006 Act, and human-elephant or human-tiger conflict near reserve borders.

In-situ conservation protects species in their natural home. Examples: national parks, sanctuaries, biosphere reserves, sacred groves. Ex-situ conservation protects them outside: zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks, gene banks, cryopreservation.

In-situ is better for whole ecosystems. Ex-situ is a backup for species on the edge.

Examples of ex-situ work include zoos regulated by the Central Zoo Authority, botanical gardens, and the National Gene Bank run by NBPGR in New Delhi. A key tool is captive breeding followed by reintroduction, as with the gharial. In-situ keeps evolution going in the wild, which ex-situ cannot copy. Most experts say the two approaches work best together, with in-situ as the main strategy.

• National Park: Section 35. Strictest. No grazing or private rights.
  • Wildlife Sanctuary: Section 26A. Some human activity may be allowed.
  • Conservation Reserve (Section 36A) and Community Reserve (Section 36C): added by the 2002 amendment on government land and community/private land.
  • Tiger Reserve: Section 38V, managed by the National Tiger Conservation Authority.

The key difference is that in a sanctuary some activities such as grazing may be permitted by the Chief Wildlife Warden, while in a national park none is allowed. Both are notified by the State government. The 2002 amendment added Conservation and Community Reserves so that people's land could be protected without taking away their rights. Tiger reserves have a core (critical tiger habitat) and a buffer where people and wildlife coexist.

The idea comes from UNESCO’s Man and the Biosphere (MAB) programme (1971). India has a national scheme from 1986 and has about 18 reserves.

Each reserve has a core zone (strictly protected), a buffer zone (limited use) and a transition zone (people live and farm). Nilgiri (1986) was first. UNESCO recognises 13 Indian reserves (Cold Desert added in 2025) in the world network, including Sundarbans, Nanda Devi, Gulf of Mannar and Khangchendzonga.

As of recent MoEFCC figures, India has over 1,000 protected areas, roughly 100 national parks and over 500 sanctuaries. They cover about 5 percent of India’s land (figures change slightly each year).

The target of 30 by 30 includes OECMs: other effective area-based measures such as community-run sites that are not formally protected.

India’s natural World Heritage Sites include Kaziranga, Manas, Keoladeo, Sundarbans, Nanda Devi and Valley of Flowers, Western Ghats and Great Himalayan National Park. Khangchendzonga is a mixed site.

World Heritage status comes from the 1972 UNESCO convention and listing does not by itself change Indian law.

The Central Zoo Authority (1992) regulates zoos. The National Bureau of Plant Genetic Resources in Delhi runs the national seed gene bank. The National Bureau of Animal Genetic Resources at Karnal holds animal genetic material.

Conservation breeding is used for the Great Indian Bustard (a centre at Jaisalmer), the gharial and vultures. The Svalbard Global Seed Vault in Norway is the world’s backup.

Critics say removing people from parks creates displacement and hostility. Supporters say core areas need inviolate space for large predators.

The Forest Rights Act 2006 recognises rights and allows Critical Wildlife Habitats. Sacred groves (Meghalaya’s Law Kyntang, Rajasthan’s Orans, Kerala’s Kavu) show that community conservation also works.

Kaziranga protects the one-horned rhino. Gir holds the Asiatic lion. Keoladeo is a Ramsar and World Heritage bird site. Simlipal and Nilgiri are biosphere reserves. Sundarbans is both a tiger reserve and biosphere reserve.

Eco-sensitive zones (ESZ) around parks regulate activity in a buffer, usually up to 10 km unless fixed otherwise.

Mains-style: “Distinguish between in-situ and ex-situ conservation. Which is better for India’s biodiversity?” Structure: definitions; examples; strengths and limits of each; they are complementary; policy (CAMPA, community reserves).

Mains-style: “Protected areas versus people: how can both be served?”

Prelims tip: Biosphere reserves are not under the WPA. Community reserves are on private or community land. National parks allow no grazing.

quiz.q: Which Section creates National Parks in the Wildlife Protection Act?
quiz.w: 26A is for sanctuaries, 36A conservation reserves and 38V tiger reserves.
Section 36C allows them on community or private land.

quiz.q: Which zone of a biosphere reserve has the least human use?
Which of these is a mixed World Heritage Site in India?
quiz.w: Khangchendzonga is listed for both natural and cultural values.

quiz.q: The national seed gene bank is run by:
quiz.w: The National Bureau of Plant Genetic Resources runs it.
Seed banks store seeds outside natural habitat.

quiz.q: Central Zoo Authority was set up in:
quiz.w: It was established in 1992 under the Wildlife Act.

quiz.q: Tiger reserves are notified under which Section?
Keoladeo National Park is famous for:
quiz.w: It is a Ramsar and World Heritage wetland in Bharatpur.
